## Summary

**Current official documentation explicitly says `UserPromptSubmit` runs on a message another session sends to the main conversation, and that this hook can block the prompt before Claude receives it.** This answers question 2 affirmatively at the documented feature level. It does **not** establish a complete authenticated inbound authorization layer: the documented hook fields do not provide an authenticated peer-sender identity or permission-class field, and the installed runtime’s event coverage has not been tested.  
Sources: [Hooks — UserPromptSubmit](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#userpromptsubmit), [common input fields](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#common-input-fields). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, official documentation. Relationship: extends the repository’s unresolved inbound-hook question.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

**The default messaging policy compares two permission-mode classes, not exact mode names.** Current documentation also provides `crossSessionInbound` controls, so making every session bypass permissions is not the only documented way to avoid a permission-class hold. Neither matching classes nor accepting inbound messages grants authority to launch workers, approve a person-only decision, or perform an otherwise forbidden action.  
Sources: [Inbound controls](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#control-inbound-messages), [settings precedence](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#crosssessioninbound), [incoming-message boundaries](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#how-a-session-treats-an-incoming-message). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, official documentation. Relationship: extends and qualifies issue #339’s proposed immediate remedy.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

**Question 1 remains partly unresolved.** Official documentation describes the supported permission-mode controls and says the sender “identifies itself” as bypassing prompts. It does not document the exact per-message permission-class identification mechanism, a supported class-assertion argument, or a wire-level verification contract. This report does not invent one.  
Sources: [Inbound controls](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#control-inbound-messages), [tools reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference), [permission modes](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes). **Relevance: HIGH. ## 1. Permission-mode classes and the “Held message” behavior

### Finding 1 — Default delivery compares classes, not exact mode names

The official messaging page groups sessions into:

1. Sessions that bypass permission prompts.
2. All other sessions.

It expressly places `auto`, `acceptEdits` and `dontAsk` in the prompting class. **Plan mode is an important exception:** it counts as bypassing in interactive terminal sessions where bypass permissions are available.

When no explicit inbound setting applies, the documented policy is:

| Receiving session’s class | Sender identifies itself as bypassing | Sender does not identify itself as bypassing |
|---|---|---|
| Prompting | Held for approval | Delivered |
| Bypassing | Delivered | Held for approval |

The second column describes what the receiver is told about the sender; it is not proof that this research knows the internal assertion or verification mechanism.

Consequently:

- Exact permission-mode equality is **not necessary** for the default to deliver.
- A matching-class expectation is **not sufficient** to guarantee end-to-end receipt: settings, outbound checks, hooks, availability, queue limits and other refusal conditions remain relevant.
- A hold does not independently prove the sender was launched in a particular mode.
- `dontAsk` is not the bypass class merely because it does not present ordinary approval prompts; the messaging documentation explicitly classifies it as prompting.

Source: [Control inbound messages](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#control-inbound-messages). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, official documentation. Relationship: extends G40 and contradicts any interpretation that exact mode names must match.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

### Finding 2 — A hold is non-delivery, not an instruction waiting inside Claude’s context

The receiving session distinguishes **Delivered**, **Held** and **Refused**. Held messages remain undelivered until approval or a qualifying later mode/settings change.

Under the permission-derived default, an interactive terminal displays an approval dialog. Approving delivers that message; denying or dismissing drops it. The default deadline is five minutes. Explicit `hold` differs: the documentation says messages held by that setting do not expire and can be released when an applicable `accept` later replaces it.

Non-interactive sessions cannot display the dialog. A default-held message can expire, and Claude Code reports expiry to a sender it can reach. The documentation also caps held messages at 100, dropping the oldest beyond that.

These rules explain a plausible mechanism for the reported symptom, but they do not reproduce the historical incident or prove its precise configuration.

Sources: [Inbound controls](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#control-inbound-messages), [non-interactive sessions](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#non-interactive-sessions), [dialog expiry](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#dialogexpiry). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, official documentation. Relationship: supports the historical hold interpretation while adding expiry and unattended-session risks.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

## 2. Question 1 — How does a sender identify itself as bypassing?

### Finding 3 — Supported mode controls are documented; the class-identification protocol is not

Official documentation describes equivalent ways to start directly in bypass mode:

- `--permission-mode bypassPermissions`
- `--dangerously-skip-permissions`

It separately documents `--allow-dangerously-skip-permissions`, which makes bypass selectable later without starting in it. Confusing availability with the currently active mode would be incorrect.

However, the messaging documentation still phrases the receiver’s condition as the sender “identifies itself” as bypassing. The reviewed messaging, permission-mode, CLI and tools references do not expose a supported per-send permission-class argument or explain the exact class-bearing wire representation and validation.

**Answer to question 1:** The supported user-facing mechanism is to configure an actual session permission mode through the product’s permission controls, not to add an assertion to message text. The exact internal mechanism by which native messaging represents that class remains **[UNVERIFIED]** from the reviewed public documentation. No undocumented flag, JSON field or socket payload is recommended.

Sources: [Bypass permission mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes#skip-all-checks-with-bypasspermissions-mode), [CLI reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference#cli-flags), [inbound controls](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#control-inbound-messages), [tools reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH for the supported interface; internal protocol unresolved. Relationship: partially answers G40 without claiming a discovered sender-class API.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

### Finding 4 — An explicit inbound policy is an alternative to changing tool-execution mode

Current documentation provides `crossSessionInbound`:

- `accept`: deliver messages to Claude.
- `hold`: show a notice without delivering.
- `refuse`: drop messages.

Its precedence is security-specific. Claude Code reads managed settings, then `--settings`, then user settings, taking the first applicable value. Project/local settings can tighten that value, but cannot loosen it; `refuse` is stricter than `hold`, which is stricter than `accept`.

This is not a named-sender trust list. The documented setting applies to inbound cross-session messages generally. The reviewed setting section does not document a parent-only or per-sender exception.

`isolatePeerMachines` is separate: a `true` from any settings scope requires explicit approval for messages beyond the machine, including in bypass mode.

**Decision implication:** accepting messages and granting tools permission are separate decisions. A future, user-approved unattended receiver could retain a non-bypass tool policy while choosing an inbound policy, subject to managed/project restrictions. That would still need message validation and authorization; it is not permission to change settings during this research.

Sources: [crossSessionInbound](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#crosssessioninbound), [isolatePeerMachines](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#isolatepeermachines), [non-interactive messaging](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#non-interactive-sessions). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, official documentation. Relationship: extends the options beyond issue #339’s all-bypass proposal.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

## 3. Question 2 — Can a hook inspect or reject inbound messages?

### Finding 5 — Yes: current documentation explicitly includes cross-session main-conversation messages

The hooks reference states:

> “`UserPromptSubmit` hooks don't fire only on prompts you type.”

It then explicitly includes:

> “A message another session sends to your main conversation”

The same section documents the submitted text in `prompt`. Returning `decision: "block"` stops the prompt before it reaches Claude; exiting with code 2 also blocks it.

**Answer to question 2:** Yes, current official documentation describes a receiving-side `UserPromptSubmit` inspection/blocking point for messages sent by another session to the main conversation. This is stronger evidence than a generic inference from the event’s name.

The supported conclusion has limits:

- It is documentation of a product feature, not a live test of this installed build.
- The section does not separately enumerate every active-turn versus idle-turn delivery path.
- It does not establish equivalent interception for every teammate, subagent, remote channel or non-Claude transport.
- An event that carries message text is not automatically an authenticated sender/authority interface.

Source: [UserPromptSubmit](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#userpromptsubmit). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, official documentation. Relationship: answers the feature-level inbound-hook uncertainty and extends G40; deployed coverage remains open.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

### Finding 6 — Hook payload identity describes the receiving execution context, not an authenticated peer sender

The common fields document:

- `session_id`: current session identifier.
- `permission_mode`: current permission mode.
- `agent_id`: the subagent or in-process teammate in which the hook fires.
- `agent_type`: the applicable agent type.
- `transcript_path`: the local conversation transcript path, whose contents can lag because writes are asynchronous.

The `UserPromptSubmit` section adds `prompt` and, when present, `session_title`. These documented fields do **not** establish an authenticated peer-sender identity, sender permission class, parent Dispatch identity, or grant chain.

Therefore a validator must not mistake:

- The receiving `session_id` for the sender’s identity.
- The receiver’s `permission_mode` for the sender’s mode.
- An `agent_id` for a verified external peer sender.
- A sender name or an identity assertion inside text for independently authenticated authority.
- A transcript file for a guaranteed current-event feed.

**[UNVERIFIED]** Whether additional trusted origin metadata exists in the installed runtime, and whether it covers the required delivery paths, remains unresolved. This is not a claim that no such metadata exists anywhere.

Sources: [Common hook fields](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#common-input-fields), [UserPromptSubmit input](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#userpromptsubmit-input). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH for the documented fields; additional metadata unverified. Relationship: supports the local finding that current launch bindings do not supply delegated role/parent authority.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

### Finding 7 — Blocking decisions and fail-closed operation are separate requirements

The hooks documentation gives `UserPromptSubmit` command, HTTP and MCP-tool hooks a default 30-second timeout. A timed-out hook ordinarily has its output discarded and the prompt continues. Command/HTTP hooks can use `onFailure: "block"` to block instead. SDK callback timeout handling is documented separately and blocks the prompt.

The source registration in H:63–70 sets a five-second timeout for the existing launch guard and does not set `onFailure: "block"`. G:142–161 contains an internal exit trap, but an internal error handler is not proof of how the host handles a hook timeout.

**[CODE-VERIFIED]** The existing source registration and guard are not a completed fail-closed typed-message validator. **[UNVERIFIED]** Installed timeout behavior, hook ordering and concurrent execution were not exercised.

Other hook types have different roles:

| Hook | What it establishes | What it does not establish |
|---|---|---|
| `PreToolUse` matching `SendMessage` | Sender-side tool-call inspection before execution | Recipient-side interception of every inbound message |
| `PostToolUse` | Inspection of the completed call and its result | Prevention or reversal of an already executed send |
| `PermissionRequest` | A decision when a tool call needs permission | A universal incoming-message event |
| `Notification` | Notification observation | A blocking message gate; documentation says it cannot block or modify notifications |

Sources: [UserPromptSubmit](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#userpromptsubmit), [PreToolUse](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#pretooluse), [PostToolUse](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#posttooluse), [PermissionRequest](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#permissionrequest), [Notification](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#notification). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, official documentation plus directly read registration/source. Relationship: extends G40 into concrete reliability requirements; does not certify existing enforcement.**

## 4. Delivery guarantees, acknowledgments, and message formats

### Finding 8 — Preserve explicit guarantees, but distinguish the three messaging mechanisms

The documentation provides meaningful delivery behavior. It must not be flattened into either “all successful sends are processed” or “nothing is guaranteed.”

**Independent cross-session messages**

- Delivered messages are read between tool calls during an active turn; a running tool is not interrupted.
- An idle recipient starts a new turn with the message.
- Inbound controls may hold or refuse it.
- Some refusals occur at the sender before the message leaves.
- For an unreachable-by-policy remote target, the tool result begins `Not sent`.
- Recipient inbox drops can produce a later report naming queue overflow, rate limits, duplicates or relay-loop protection.
- Default-held non-interactive messages can expire.

The cross-session and tools pages reviewed do not provide a universal positive tool-return guarantee of recipient reading, application, task completion, or eventual execution.

**Agent-team mailbox messages**

The team architecture page makes an explicit tool-result guarantee:

> “Claude Code reports a message as sent only when the write to the recipient's mailbox file succeeds”

It also says a failed write returns an error and nothing is sent. **This is a mailbox-write guarantee for that mechanism**, not proof that the recipient read, accepted, applied or completed the requested work, and not a reason to transplant team-file semantics onto independent peer sockets.

**Final subagent reports**

In auto mode, a flagged final report is still delivered with a security warning, or a verification note if the classifier is unavailable. This is a distinct handback guarantee, not the behavior of every blocked `SendMessage`.

Sources: [Cross-session delivery](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#message-delivery), [inbox-drop errors](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/errors#cross-session-message-was-dropped-at-the-recipient-sessions-inbox), [team architecture](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams#architecture), [auto-mode subagent review](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes#eliminate-prompts-with-auto-mode), [tools reference](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, official documentation. Relationship: supports retaining explicit application acknowledgments and result admission rather than treating a send return as completion.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

**[CODE-VERIFIED]** K:61 already requires `applied|queued|refused` acknowledgments for coordinator follow-ups. K:103–108 separately describes Delivery handling, sender Task/Dispatch validation and completion processing. K:138 explicitly says an acknowledgment does not prove the answer was right. These current policies are compatible with the external distinction between transport receipt and application-level acceptance; they are not proof that Claude-native peer messaging supplies Orca’s lifecycle semantics.

### Finding 9 — Typed application messages are possible, but are not a built-in cross-session authorization protocol

Independent cross-session messaging is documented as **plain text only**. Structured team protocol messages remain within a team. File/MCP mentions in peer text do not attach the referenced contents, and a slash command arrives as text rather than being automatically executed.

Therefore an application could define a structured text envelope, but merely choosing fields such as `type`, worktree and branch would not provide:

- Trusted sender identity.
- Authorization for the requested operation.
- Replay protection.
- Correct lifecycle settlement.
- Enforcement that a free-text detail field never influences later behavior.

Those are design requirements, not features delivered by naming a fixed set of message types.

**[CODE-VERIFIED]** K:101 lists the current Orca message vocabulary; K:105–106 requires handling unknown types and checking relevant sender Task/Dispatch identities. An independent Claude-native text envelope is not automatically that protocol.

Sources: [Cross-session limitations](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#limitations), [incoming-message handling](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#how-a-session-treats-an-incoming-message), [message delivery](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#message-delivery). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, official documentation plus directly read policy. Relationship: qualifies G41 and extends issue #339’s typed-message proposal without claiming it exists.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

### Finding 10 — Idle notifications can reduce checking, but cannot replace supervision

The documented `notify_when_idle` subscription is:

- One-shot.
- Restricted to main conversations watching other sessions on the same machine.
- Triggered when a turn finishes with nothing queued, or when the session exits.
- Subject to inbound controls.
- Expired after 12 hours if no notice arrives.

An idle notice is not proof of a successful task, admitted report, settled subtree, clean worktree, or authorization to close a session.

**[CODE-VERIFIED]** K:110–113 uses worker-specific evidence and semantic progress, not mere message arrival. K:151 requires targeted probes; K:157 rejects heartbeats, nudges and context exhaustion as sufficient stall proof. The native idle feature is an optional signal, not an equivalent replacement for those duties.

Source: [Get a notice when another session goes idle](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#get-a-notice-when-another-session-goes-idle). **Relevance: MEDIUM. Reliability: HIGH, official documentation. Relationship: extends the available observation signals while supporting the current distinction between liveness and completion.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

## 5. Permission laundering, auto mode, and hierarchy

### Finding 11 — Message acceptance is not consent or delegated authority

Official documentation expressly says another session’s message:

- Cannot approve a pending permission prompt.
- Cannot supply the person’s consent.
- Must not cause changes to permission settings, `CLAUDE.md` or configuration.
- Remains subject to the recipient’s permissions when acted upon.

It also instructs the sender not to route an action to another session when its own permission settings denied or would block that action.

Auto mode separately reviews outbound `SendMessage` content before delivery. A blocked message does not reach the recipient. That is different from the warning-prefixed delivery of a flagged final subagent report.

Bypass mode is not a prompt-injection defense or an isolation boundary. The official warning recommends isolated environments and says bypass offers no protection against prompt injection or unintended actions.

Sources: [Incoming-message boundaries](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#how-a-session-treats-an-incoming-message), [cross-session delivery boundaries](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#message-delivery), [team message checks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams#messages-between-agents), [permission modes](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes#skip-all-checks-with-bypasspermissions-mode). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, official documentation. Relationship: supports the existing person-only boundaries and contradicts interpreting mode alignment as a trustless grant.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

**[CODE-VERIFIED]** K:57 preserves person-only Rulings; K:41–44 limits worker outward actions and local commits; K:62 preserves the fan-out prohibition. External messaging functionality does not supersede those rules.

### Finding 12 — Native subagents, teams, and independently launched coordinators have different limits

Current official documentation distinguishes:

| Mechanism | Documented structure | Relevance to the decision |
|---|---|---|
| Subagents | Work inside a session; current docs allow bounded nesting by default | Product-level nesting capability is not Orca worker-session authority |
| Agent teams | Separate teammate contexts, with a lead; experimental; no nested teams | Not a documented turnkey orchestrator-of-orchestrators |
| Independent cross-session messaging | Separate sessions exchange text, without requiring a team relationship | Provides communication, not parent ownership, admission or subtree recovery |

Subagent permission inheritance is also constrained by the main conversation’s mode. A definition that names bypass is not a general route to elevate a non-bypass parent’s child. These subagent rules must not be applied as assumed inheritance rules for independently launched Orca sessions.

Sources: [Subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents), [agent-team limitations](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams#limitations), [cross-session messaging](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging). **Relevance: HIGH. Reliability: HIGH, official documentation. Relationship: supports distinguishing O5 internal decomposition from O3/O4 external hierarchy; does not authorize any option.**

## 6. Community patterns and implementation examples

### Finding 13 — Examples add useful context, but do not close the authorization gap

The official Python Agent SDK hook example demonstrates generic hook registration, context injection and tool-use denial. It does not demonstrate authenticated recipient-side cross-session validation. Its example therefore supports the hook mechanism, not a claim that a complete peer-message validator is already available.

Source: [Official SDK hook examples](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-agent-sdk-python/blob/main/examples/hooks.py). **Relevance: MEDIUM. Reliability: HIGH as a primary example repository; not proof of this installation or complete security behavior. Relationship: extends implementation context only.**  
<!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

The community cross-session guide was also examined. Its retrieved permission-class wording places plan mode with bypass available among prompting cases, whereas the current official page explicitly classifies the relevant interactive-terminal plan case as bypassing. Authenticated sender metadata and installed route coverage remain unverified. **HIGH relevance; HIGH reliability; extends.** [Source](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#userpromptsubmit). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->
- **Question 1 is only partly answered:** supported permission-mode controls are documented; the native sender-class identification protocol is not. Do not invent an assertion field or equate message text with mode identity. **HIGH relevance; HIGH reliability for the interface; extends.** [Sources](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#control-inbound-messages), [CLI](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cli-reference#cli-flags). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

## Recommendations from External Research

1. **Do not adopt “make every session bypass permissions” as the default remedy.** The current product separates inbound handling from tool mode. Preserve the intended tool restrictions and consider any inbound-policy choice only through explicit user/administrator approval, with its broader acceptance scope understood. **HIGH relevance; recommendation grounded in HIGH-reliability official sources; extends.** [Inbound setting](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference#crosssessioninbound), [bypass risks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes#skip-all-checks-with-bypasspermissions-mode). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

2. **Update the decision evidence, not the runtime:** record question 2 as “documented yes, deployment and security adequacy unverified,” and question 1 as “supported mode controls known, internal class-identification mechanism unresolved.” This avoids both obsolete “no inbound hook” claims and unsupported “complete inbound security layer” claims. **HIGH relevance; HIGH-reliability evidence; extends.** [Hooks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#userpromptsubmit), [inbound rules](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#control-inbound-messages). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

3. **Keep external sub-orchestrator authority gated.** Messaging and prompt interception do not justify relaxing WC-13, treating ownership wording as a grant, or bypassing person-only approvals. Any future decision needs trusted parent/scope binding, fail-closed validation, aggregate-result admission and parent-failure ownership. This is a decision prerequisite, not authorization to build those mechanisms now. **HIGH relevance; recommendation supported by HIGH-reliability product boundaries and directly read local policy; supports.** [Message boundaries](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#how-a-session-treats-an-incoming-message), [hook failure behavior](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks#userpromptsubmit). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

4. **Retain separate evidence for send, receive, apply and complete.** Do not replace existing application acknowledgments, report reading or result admission with a successful send or idle notice. Use the strongest documented guarantee for each channel without transferring it to another channel. **HIGH relevance; HIGH-reliability evidence; supports.** [Team mailbox guarantee](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-teams#architecture), [cross-session delivery](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#message-delivery), [idle notices](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#get-a-notice-when-another-session-goes-idle). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->

5. **Carry B1/B2 forward unchanged in the decision report.** Launch authority, upward communication and required supervision probes are separate integration questions. Do not broaden the literal-`orca` classifier evidence into an all-executable claim, or treat an enforcement ceiling as permission. **HIGH relevance; directly verified local evidence; supports.** The corresponding external principle is that each receiving session retains its own permission boundaries: [source](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cross-session-messaging#message-delivery). <!-- web-provenance: provider=WebSearch reason=tavily-unavailable -->
